strengths: Addresses a relevant question for human-in-the-loop NLP: how researchers’ collaboration workflows affect induced codebooks and automated document assignments.
Compares three substantially different systems on a common corpus of approximately 85,000 tweets, with fixed starting partitions within each system and participation from 20 researchers.

Combines overlap and embedding metrics with 1,200 manually evaluated document–theme pairs, double annotation and adjudication, and participant interviews. These provide useful complementary descriptive evidence.
The manuscript is generally clear and supplies useful methodological material, including prompt templates, selected model configurations, and the interview script.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not implement asynchronous collaboration as defined in the introduction. Section 4 compares three individual coders with two three-person synchronous groups per system, without consolidating the individual codebooks. Consequently, differences conflate collaboration mode with the number of contributors to each codebook. An asynchronous team condition with consolidation, or substantial reframing around individual versus group coding, is needed.

The statistical evidence is insufficiently specified. Each system has only two synchronous codebooks, yielding one between-group consistency comparison. Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without sample sizes or explaining how dependencies among themes, shared codebooks, and repeated participants are handled. Treating theme-level measurements as independent experimental replications would overstate evidence. Exact p-values, uncertainty estimates, and treatment of multiple comparisons are also missing; 'near statistically significant' results do not establish an effect.

Correctness evaluation is not reproducible from the description. Figure 4 reports F1, but the paper describes binary judgments of proposed document–theme pairs without defining the F1 calculation or averaging procedure. Treatment of unlabeled outputs is unclear, despite invalid LLM labels affecting 0.7–16.1% of documents in Table 4. Additionally, the claim that asynchronous topic modeling produces more accurate assignments is not generally supported by Figure 4: full-sample scores are equal, and synchronous scores are higher at the middle thresholds.

The proposed evaluation framework needs stronger validation. Maximum-match consistency leaves matching direction, one-to-one constraints, and unmatched themes unspecified; theme counts and sizes are also unreported. These choices can obscure differences in codebook granularity. Centroid similarities of approximately 0.94–0.98 provide limited discrimination, and their relationship to expert judgments of thematic quality is not established.

Several explanations and recommendations exceed the evidence. The hypothesis that richer interaction operations produce greater benefits from deliberation is not isolated from architecture, initialization, or the relational system’s additional stance and morality information. Broad conclusions about LLM reliability and scalability rest on one Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct configuration. The single dataset and single implementation per category support narrower conclusions about the tested setups.

Important reporting gaps remain despite the useful appendices: participant allocation and reuse across the 27 participant slots, condition order, annotation effort, the S-BERT checkpoint, LLM decoding settings, and selected prompts per codebook. The interview sample size and analysis procedure are also unspecified, and Appendix C acknowledges missing interviews. Together with the design and evaluation concerns, these prevent a clear soundness and reproducibility case for Findings; I recommend revision for the next cycle.
